s: Five applied-ML builds from before and alongside the production work. They were good for learning the tools and they were not production systems. Both halves of that are worth saying.
b: Most portfolios present work like this as though it were equivalent to production engineering. It is not, and pretending otherwise is the fastest way to lose the trust of anyone who has done both. So: here is what these were, and what I actually got out of them. What they are Multi agent content generation — a researcher agent and a writer agent coordinated through an orchestration framework to produce an article from a topic. Streamlit front end, search API for retrieval. Chat with your PDFs — retrieval augmented generation over a document collection, with a vector index and an LLM answering from retrieved chunks. Voice translation with cloning — English speech in, six languages out, preserving the speaker's voice, by chaining a transcription API and a synthesis API. Medical image chat — a vision language model answering questions about an uploaded image, with selectable backends and a chat interface. Groq chatbot — a chat application with a separate API backend and front end, containerised and deployed, with conversation history and token accounting. What they actually taught me The useful thing was not the models. It was everything around them. Containerising the chatbot and having it fail in deployment was worth more than the chatbot. The difference between "works on my machine" and "works in a container somebody else runs" is where most of the real content is, and I would not have learned it by reading. Token accounting in the Groq project turned out to be direct preparation for building a cost model over hundreds of thousands of production usage rows — including the i

s: A multi-tenant system where customers order food by chatting on WhatsApp, an LLM agent builds the cart and takes payment, and the order lands in the restaurant's point-of-sale. Several established food and beverage brands run on it.
b: A customer opens WhatsApp, messages a restaurant, and has a conversation. At the end of it there is an order in the restaurant's point of sale system, paid for, with the right modifiers on the right items going to the right branch. Nobody on the restaurant side typed anything. That is the product. Everything below is what it takes to make that reliable enough that a business will run on it. Why this is harder than it sounds The difficulty is not the conversation. Language models are good at conversation. The difficulty is that the conversation terminates in a transaction , and transactions have no tolerance for the things models are bad at. A model that invents a menu item produces a customer expecting food that does not exist. A model that attaches the wrong modifier identifier produces an order the kitchen cannot fill. A model that confirms an order it never placed produces a customer waiting for a delivery that will never arrive — and we did deliver fourteen of those before the guards that now prevent it existed. So the system is built around a single question: where is the model allowed to decide, and where does it have to prove its claim against the database? t: The schedule fired twice an hour, not every fifty-five minutes
s: `*/55 * * * *` does not mean "every 55 minutes." It means minute 0 and minute 55. The job it scheduled rewrote a 30,000-token cache each time, for months.
p: A step value in a cron field steps within that field's range and resets at its boundary. Any interval that does not divide its unit evenly does not mean what it reads like.
b: The expression /55 Read casually, that is "every fifty five minutes." It is not. The step applies within the minute field, which runs 0–59, and resets at the top of every hour. So it fires at minute 0 and minute 55 — twice an hour, five minutes apart, then a fifty five minute gap. Any step that does not divide its field's range evenly has this property. /55 , /7 , /45 all read like intervals and behave like a short pair followed by a long gap. What it was scheduling A job that mints the agent's cached system prompt — the menu, the tool definitions, the whole bilingual catalogue — so that no customer's turn has to pay the cold creation cost. Each mint writes roughly 30,000 tokens. Cache writes bill at the full input rate. There was a second defect layered on it: the job re minted unconditionally, without checking whether the current cache was still live and its inputs unchanged. So the extra firings were not merely extra, they were entirely redundant. ~840 cache writes/day → ~384 Why nothing caught it Every individual component reported success. The job ran, the cache was created, the customer facing behaviour was correct — arguably better than correct, since the cache was always extremely fresh. The only symptom was money, in a line item that was itself being mis attributed by a factor of 3.8 /ahmedamer/lessons/cost dashboard overstated by 3.8x/ . A cost bug hiding inside a cost reporting bug is not a coincidence — the reason nobody was scrutinising the cache write line was that the whole spend figure was known to be untrustworthy. ::: principle Waste does not raise. t: A tool's return value is conversation history, forever
s: An instruction written into a tool's return string — "do not call this again" — was replayed into every subsequent turn, so the agent obeyed a months-old prohibition and silently sent nothing.
p: Turn-local state belongs in process state, policy belongs in the system prompt, and neither belongs in a tool's return value. Whatever a tool returns is replayed as history for the life of the conversation.
b: The bug A tool that sends a product carousel returned a string that ended, roughly: Carousel sent successfully. Do not call this tool again for this category. The intent was reasonable: stop the agent from sending the same carousel twice in one turn. The instruction worked perfectly for that, and then kept working, for the rest of the conversation's life. Why it persists A tool call and its result are appended to the message history. That history is replayed into the model on every subsequent turn. So an instruction placed in a return value is not a one time signal to the current turn — it is a permanent addition to the conversation's context, carrying the same authority as everything else in it. Weeks later, a customer asking to see that category again produced an agent that consulted its history, found a clear instruction not to call the tool, and complied. The symptom was worse than not sending It did not fail loudly. It did not fail at all, in any sense a monitoring system could detect. The agent called no tool, so there was no tool error. It produced a reply, so there was no empty response event. The reply was a paraphrase of the example sentence from the tool's own description, because that was the most relevant text about carousels in its context. So the customer asked to see the menu, and received a sentence about menus, and no menu. Nothing was logged, because from the system's point of view a turn completed normally. ::: principle An agent that decides not to act produces no error. The absence of a tool call is indistinguishable from a turn that legitimately neede

t: Catching an exception does not contain it
s: A best-effort helper that swallowed its own errors still broke the caller's next query, because the failed statement had already marked the transaction for rollback. It never reproduced locally, for an instructive reason.
p: A caught database exception still poisons the surrounding transaction. Only a savepoint contains it — try/except contains the control flow, not the connection state.
b: The surprising part python try: Thing.objects.create payload=value value has the wrong type except Exception: pass best effort, never raises This function does not raise. It also breaks the caller's next query, and the one after that, until the request ends. Once a statement fails inside a transaction, the connection is marked as needing rollback. Catching the Python exception changes what happens to your control flow. It does not change what the database now thinks about this transaction. Every subsequent query raises, and the traceback points at code that is completely fine. The fix is a savepoint — an atomic block around the fallible statement — so the failure rolls back only to that point: python try: with transaction.atomic : Thing.objects.create payload=value except Exception: logger.warning "…", exc info=True ::: principle try/except around a database write contains the exception, not the transaction. If a helper is described as "never raises," it needs a savepoint, or the promise is only true for its own caller and false for everyone after it. ::: Why it never reproduced locally This is the part I would want somebody else to take away. The helper's first action is a call to a vector search service. On developer machines, that service was not running. So the helper failed early, returned, and never reached the insert that was the actual bug. The bug was structurally unreachable in every environment where anybody could have found it, because a dependency was broken there. ::: principle A locally broken dependency does not just hide bugs behind it — it makes them unrea

t: I was wrong three times before I asked the right question
s: Messages were disappearing. Three careful hypotheses, all disproven, before a single query settled it. The generalisable move is asking what the earliest thing you write down is, before your own logic can discard anything.
p: When input goes missing, query the earliest artifact you persist before business logic runs. Everything downstream cannot distinguish "never arrived" from "arrived and was discarded."
b: Three wrong answers Messages were not being replied to. I had three hypotheses, in order, each reasonable and each supported by something: 1. The queue is losing them. Plausible — there had been a redelivery incident before. Disproven by the queue metrics. 2. The platform is not calling us. Plausible — configuration drifts, tokens expire, apps sit in development mode. Disproven, eventually, but it took longest because our own runbook recommends it. 3. A worker is crashing mid turn. Plausible — an out of memory kill would produce exactly this shape, with the message redelivered and lost again. Disproven by the absence of restarts. All three were careful. All three were wrong. The fourth thing I did took one query. What the queue metrics said This is the part worth keeping, because the metrics were not broken. They were accurate and they were irrelevant. sent 32 received 32 deleted 32 dead letter queue empty Thirty two in, thirty two out, nothing parked. A perfect record — of the messages that made it as far as the queue. The discard was happening inside the consuming process, after the message had been received and before anything was written down. From the queue's point of view that is indistinguishable from successful processing, because the process did acknowledge it. It just did not do anything first. ::: principle "Received and deleted" means a process took responsibility for a message. It does not mean the message produced an effect. Those are different claims, and only the second one is what you care about. ::: The question that worked Eventually I asked something dif

t: The security guard was turning away customers, nondeterministically
s: A printed QR code produced a prefilled message that asserted a role. The prompt-injection classifier read it as an attack and deflected 132 of 730 arrivals in a month — on byte-identical input, inconsistently.
p: Before a classifier can block anything, enumerate the legitimate inputs that structurally resemble an attack. Your own system generates some of them.
b: Two things were true at once The prompt injection classifier was working. It was also turning away roughly one in six people who scanned a QR code in a restaurant. Those are not in tension. The classifier was doing exactly what it was asked: judge whether a message is trying to manipulate the assistant's instructions. The QR code's prefilled message asserts a role. It genuinely looks like an injection attempt. It was written by us. The metric that pointed the wrong way The deflection count is the obvious health metric for an injection guard, and it is almost useless on its own. It goes up when you are being attacked and it goes up when you are blocking customers, and it does not distinguish the two. What made this visible was not the counter. It was noticing that identical input produced different verdicts across runs. A rule cannot do that. Only a judgement near a decision boundary can. ::: principle If a classifier returns different verdicts for byte identical input, it is not applying a rule — it is expressing an opinion. That is fine for ranking and unacceptable for blocking. ::: The design that came out of it The fix was not a better prompt or a bigger model. It was removing the need for a judgement wherever a decision was already knowable. Anything the system generates itself is known safe by construction — we wrote it. A bare number, a star rating, a location line has no room to carry an instruction. Those go through an exact match allowlist and never reach the classifier. Two rules keep that safe. Exact match after normalisation , never substring or prefix, so appen

t: The cost dashboard was wrong by 3.8x, confidently
s: We were reporting $6,712 of model spend against $1,767 of actual spend, because the pricing treated cached input tokens as an addition to input tokens rather than a discounted subset of them.
p: Derive a billing model from the provider's own usage rows, not from the shape the API response suggests. A plausible reading of a field is not a measurement of it.
b: The error For eight months the internal dashboard reported roughly $6,700 of model spend. The actual figure was roughly $1,770. Being wrong by 3.8× in the direction of overstating cost sounds harmless. It is not. Every decision that spend informed was made against a number that was almost four times too large: which model to use, whether caching was worth its complexity, whether a feature could afford another call. A confidently wrong number is worse than an absent one, because an absent one gets questioned. Why it was wrong The usage response reports input tokens and cached tokens . There are two readings: Addition — total input is input + cached , and cached tokens are extra. Subset — cached is the portion of input that came from cache, billed cheaper. We had implemented the first. The truth is the second. And because cached input bills at about a tenth of fresh input, while 96.2% of our input was cache reads, the two readings diverge by almost exactly the factor we observed. The documentation is not especially explicit about this. But the data is. The move that settled it Rather than reading the documentation more carefully, I tested the relationship against every usage row in the database. The subset hypothesis makes a falsifiable prediction: cached tokens input tokens should be impossible . The addition hypothesis makes it commonplace. rows examined 391,479 rows where cached input 0 Zero in 391,479 is not ambiguous. ::: principle When two readings of an API field imply different invariants, find the invariant that one of them forbids and test it against your own data.

t: The 466 MB directory that reports as 296 KB
s: A container image was heavy because of a directory the usual size command says is tiny. Sparse files have an apparent size and an allocated size, and a build context archives the apparent one.
p: Measure the thing the consumer measures. A build context archives apparent size; the tool you reach for reports allocated size. They are different numbers for the same directory.
b: The contradiction An image layer was 466 MB larger than the files it should have contained. Checking the suspect directory: $ du sh qdrant storage/ 296K Both measurements were correct. Two sizes for one file A sparse file has holes: regions that read as zeros but occupy no blocks on disk. A vector database preallocates large files this way. So the file has two sizes: Allocated — the blocks actually on disk. This is what du reports, and what your disk usage is. Apparent — the length of the file as far as any reader is concerned. This is what ls l reports, and what anything that reads the file end to end has to handle. A container build context is a reader. It archives the file, which means it reads all of it, including the holes, and writes out the zeros. 296 KB on disk became 233 MB in the build context and 466 MB in the layer. ::: principle Disk usage and transfer size are different quantities, and for sparse files they differ by orders of magnitude. When a size is surprising, check which of the two your tool is reporting and which one the consumer cares about. ::: One line in the build exclusions took the image from 1.8 GB to 1.32 GB. The metric that was actually wrong Total image size turned out to be the wrong headline anyway. What a deploy costs is not the size of the image, it is the size of the layers that are not already cached on the target. Almost all of that 1.8 GB was stable base layers that never move. The number that determines how long a deploy takes is the uncached tail, and that went from 565 MB to 78 MB — roughly a sevenfold faster deploy cycle, from a cha

t: The security signal went to zero and both explanations are bad
s: A steady 3.4% prompt-injection deflection rate fell to zero over two days. No deploy, no model change, no errors. Either detection went dark, or we had been turning away real customers for weeks. I still do not know which.
p: A monitored rate falling to zero is an event. Design the alert for "this signal stopped" as carefully as the one for "this signal spiked."
b: What I know A rate that had been stable for as long as it had been measured went to zero, over two days, and stayed there. The classifier is still running. It is invoked on essentially every turn, its spans record success, its error count is unchanged at zero to two a day, it resolves to the same model, and no deploy touched it in the window. The deflections it used to produce came from roughly ninety different customers a day, about one per conversation, so it was not one determined attacker who got bored. Everything mechanical I can test comes back normal. The guard is running and it is returning safe, always. Why both explanations are bad If the model drifted , then our prompt injection detection is now effectively disabled, and nothing in the system registered that. The model identifier is the same string; the behaviour behind it is not something we control or can pin. This is the worse operational outcome, and it is the one the fail open design makes hardest to notice — a guard that is not catching anything and a guard that has nothing to catch produce identical telemetry. If the classifier was false positiving all along , then for weeks we were deflecting around 3.4% of real customers with a polite refusal to engage, and something upstream changed to stop feeding it the inputs it got wrong. This is the worse product outcome, and there is a candidate: a fix landed near this window that stopped a QR code prefill from reaching the classifier at all. But "near" is not "because," and I have not established the causal link. Why the stored data cannot settle it This is the p

t: I wrote a careful latency analysis, then measured it and two conclusions flipped
s: Six prioritised recommendations, reconstructed from log timestamps. When the tracing arrived, one was inverted, one was overstated by 3x, and the largest problem in the system was not in the document at all.
p: An estimate reconstructed from adjacent data is a hypothesis. Label it as one, and keep it visible after the measurement so the correction is legible.
b: The document Before the tracing existed I wrote an analysis of where an agent turn's time was going. It had six prioritised fixes, each with an estimated saving and a rationale. It was cited in planning. It was careful work. It was reconstructed from timestamps in token logs, which bracket model calls and nothing else. What measurement did to it Two conclusions inverted, one was out by a factor of three, and the single largest problem in the system did not appear anywhere in it. The inversion is the one I think about most. The document recommended disabling the model's reasoning budget on the main call, reasoning that it was pure overhead on a conversational turn. The spans showed that a greeting spends about 120 reasoning tokens, while a complex multi item order spends 627. So the saving is smallest exactly where disabling it would be safe — on a greeting — and largest exactly where the reasoning is doing the work that keeps an order correct. That recommendation is now marked not done, deliberately , which is a stronger statement than not done . The thing the technique could not see Reconstructing from token logs means your measurement surface is exactly the set of things that write token logs. Model calls do. Prompt construction does not. So prompt construction had an implied cost of zero in every estimate in the document. It was, in fact, 19,369 database queries and about a third of all turn time /ahmedamer/lessons/menu that cost 19369 queries/ . ::: principle Any measurement reconstructed from a proxy can only see what the proxy emits. Everything silent is scored zero,

s: The single largest latency problem in the product was not in the latency document, because nobody had measured it. One translated label, one query — repeated across the whole catalogue, on every turn.
p: An N+1 is invisible on a development dataset and linear in production data. Profile against a realistic catalogue, not a seeded one.
b: The number One call to render a menu: 19,369 database queries, about 30 seconds. After the fix, the same call, producing byte identical output: 12 queries. Why nobody had noticed Translatable text — product names, category names, descriptions — lives in separate per language tables. Resolving one label means one lookup. The renderer did that lookup per label, unprefetched, in a loop. On a development database with a dozen products this is imperceptible. On a real catalogue it is linear in the number of labels, and a bilingual menu has a great many labels. The cost only exists at production scale, which is exactly where nobody was running a query counter. It got worse than a single render. A tool whose entire job was to return the details of one item built the whole bilingual menu and then scanned it for the identifier it wanted. One call: 19,369 queries and 7.66 seconds, to look up one product. A six item bundle did it six times — 116,214 queries, 52.7 seconds. The part that was not a performance bug While fixing this I found something worse in the same code path, and it had nothing to do with speed. One prompt built its menu without the tenant scope and in a language string that matched no stored row. So every label resolution failed and fell back to a placeholder. All 165 modifier groups and 2,720 options reached the model as ModifierGroup <id — nameless. That prompt's job was repairing incorrect modifier identifiers. It was being asked to correct identifiers while being shown nothing but identifiers. Fixing the scope took the prompt from 344,551 characters to 47,566 — ro

t: Meta stopped sending the phone number, and we dropped the message silently
s: WhatsApp began rolling out usernames. Senders who adopted one arrived with no phone number in the payload, our ingest discarded them with a bare continue, and nobody found out from an alert.
p: A guard that discards input must log what it discarded. Silence is indistinguishable from the case never occurring, and platform contracts change without asking you.
b: What happened WhatsApp started letting people use a username instead of exposing their phone number. For a sender who adopts one, the inbound webhook simply does not contain a phone number. The identity lives in different fields. Our parser read the phone field, found nothing, and skipped the message. One line, no logging: python if not from number: continue Nothing raised. Nothing was recorded. The error rate did not move, the queues stayed clean, the dead letter queues stayed empty, and the dashboards stayed green. Around twenty customers a day, across seven tenants, were messaging restaurants and being met with silence. Why our own runbook made it worse We had a documented procedure for "this number has gone quiet." Its second step is to count the inbound messages ever seen for that tenant, and if the count has not moved, conclude that Meta is not calling us and go and look at the platform configuration. That step is right for every cause we had previously encountered — a webhook subscription that was never made, an app left in development mode, an expired token. It is precisely wrong here, because Meta was calling us, on time, with a valid payload. The count did not move because we deleted the evidence ourselves, four lines before we would have recorded it. ::: principle A diagnostic step that distinguishes "they did not call" from "they called and we discarded it" has to read the earliest artifact you persist — the one written before any of your own logic can throw it away. Anything further downstream cannot tell the two apart. ::: The runbook now begins by querying th

t: The same change measured as a 6.8-second win and a 1.2-second loss
s: Benchmarking against a remote model by running one arm then the other lets the provider's own load drift decide the result. Twice it decided wrongly, in opposite directions.
p: Any A/B against a service you do not control must interleave its arms and report a second quantity that does not depend on the network.
b: The numbers One code change. Three ways of measuring it: | Method | Before | After | Conclusion it supports | | | | | | | sequential, n=4, quiet API | 11.52 s | 4.74 s | ship it, huge win | | sequential, n=6, congested API | 13.06 s | 14.21 s | revert it, regression | | interleaved, n=8 per arm | 8.38 s | 5.81 s | ship it, −2.57 s | The first two are the same experiment run at different times of day. They disagree about the sign. Why sequential designs fail here A remote model's latency is not a property of your request. It is a property of your request and everyone else's, at that moment, on that provider's hardware. That component drifts on a timescale of minutes to hours — and for most changes worth making, it drifts by more than the change is worth. Run all of arm A and then all of arm B, and every bit of that drift lands in the difference between them. You are not measuring your change; you are measuring your change plus whatever happened to the provider in between, with no way to separate the two. Interleaving does not remove the drift. It distributes it across both arms, so it shows up as variance rather than as bias. The part that makes it trustworthy Interleaving alone would still have left me with two numbers and a hope. What settled it was finding a quantity that measures the same change and cannot be contaminated by network conditions. At temperature zero, the model's thinking token counts were perfectly stable: 851 on every call in one arm, 367 on every call in the other. Not an average — the same value each time. Against a separately measured rate of 4.44 seco

t: The slowest thing in the system was the thing protecting it
s: The order validator took 10.38 seconds on average — more than twice the agent turn it guards. The cause was not the model. It was reasoning nobody had capped, and measuring it correctly required interleaving the two arms.
p: When a model call is slow, measure its thinking tokens before you change the model. The budget is usually the variable, and it is the one you control.
b: The finding The guard cost more than the thing it guarded. Not marginally: the order validator averaged 10.38 seconds against the agent's 4.61, on a call that runs after the work is already done, while a customer waits. Why the obvious fix was the wrong first move The validator runs on a stronger model than the agent does, and that is a defensible choice — a checker weaker than the thing it checks is decorative. So "the model is too big" is the natural hypothesis, and it leads directly to an expensive experiment: swap the model, build an evaluation harness, measure how much accuracy you lose, argue about whether the trade is worth it. Attributing the time first took an afternoon and made that experiment unnecessary. Seventy per cent of the call was reasoning tokens, and the reasoning budget had never been set. Every other model call in the system passed one explicitly. This one was written later and simply did not, so the provider's default applied — on a very large prompt, several times per order. ::: principle Before changing which model runs a slow call, find out what fraction of it is reasoning. The budget is a parameter you control; the model is a decision with accuracy consequences. Check the cheap variable first. ::: The measurement nearly lied twice I want to dwell on the verification, because it produced two confident, opposite, completely wrong answers before it produced the right one. The natural way to A/B a latency change is to run the control arm, then the treatment arm, and compare. I did that, at a quiet time, and got a 6.8 second improvement — far too large

t: We told the agent to sell something that did not exist
s: A cluster of conversations where the agent invented offers had a single, entirely non-AI cause: a configuration field instructing it to reference a promotion that only existed on a different tenant's menu.
p: When a model hallucinates consistently in one domain, audit what its configuration promises against what its data contains. Instructing a model to cite a nonexistent thing while forbidding invention leaves it one option.
b: The shape of the mistake I made Eight conversations where the agent offered a promotion that could not be ordered. My first pass classified them as the model substituting a similar item for a missing one — a known failure mode, plausible, and completely wrong. That misclassification cost real time, because it pointed at prompt engineering and retrieval quality. The actual cause was a row in a settings table. What was actually there A per tenant free text configuration field, injected verbatim into the system prompt, says roughly: there is an active promotion running, refer the customer to the menu item called X , and do not make up any offer details that are not provided. There is no menu item called X on that tenant. There is exactly one product with that name anywhere in the database, and it belongs to a different restaurant entirely — a separate tenant with a separate catalogue. So the instruction set is: 1. Tell customers about X . 2. Do not invent details about X . 3. X does not exist. These cannot all be satisfied. The model took the first instruction as binding, since it was the actionable one, and supplied the details from the nearest thing it could find — producing a price borrowed from an unrelated promotion, five confident affirmations that the offer existed, one denial, and then another affirmation. ::: principle An instruction to cite something, combined with a prohibition on invention, combined with the thing's absence, is not three constraints. It is a contradiction, and the model will resolve it by inventing. The guardrail against hallucination was part of t

t: Two machines were running the same scheduler, and customers got everything twice
s: The scheduling tool writes per-host entries, so every instance that boots installs its own copy. Two boxes meant two of every sweep — including the ones that message customers.
p: A scheduler that installs itself at boot has no concept of a fleet. Exactly-one has to be enforced by a lease, not by the number of machines you believe you have.
b: The signature Rows arriving in pairs, about 28 seconds apart, on a schedule meant to produce one. That gap is not a jitter setting or a retry — it is the difference between when two machines finished booting. Once you have seen that signature it is unmistakable. A duplicate caused by a retry clusters tightly or backs off exponentially. A duplicate caused by two independent schedulers sits at a fixed, arbitrary offset that never changes, because it is the distance between two clocks that were started at different moments and are otherwise running correctly. Why the tool cannot help The scheduling library writes into the host's own crontab. That is entirely reasonable for one machine and has no meaning at all for a group of them. There is no coordination, because from the tool's point of view there is nothing to coordinate with — it does not know other hosts exist. The instance startup script installs the schedule at boot. So the number of schedulers is the number of instances, and the number of instances is an autoscaling decision nobody thinks of as a scheduling decision. ::: principle Any component that installs itself at boot scales with your fleet whether or not that makes sense. Ask of every boot time action: what happens if this runs on three machines at once? ::: What actually matters here The duplicate snapshot rows are harmless — a monitoring table with twice the rows it needs. The same schedule also runs the customer facing sweeps. Abandoned cart reminders. Browse reminders. Order follow ups. Those went out twice, to real people, and no counter anywhere reflects th

t: The guard blocked more orders than the bug it was built to stop
s: A safety stage added to stop the agent from confirming orders it had never placed turned out to be rejecting two-thirds of legitimate orders. Its unit tests passed because they stubbed the exact component that was broken.
p: A stage whose verdict nothing can corroborate is the stage that will produce your false positives, however carefully its prompt is written.
b: The comfortable version of this story An AI agent sometimes confirmed orders it had not actually placed. We built a guard. The guard worked. Both sentences are true. The guard did catch hallucinated payment methods and modifier identifiers belonging to other products. It is still in the system. What is missing is that while it was catching those, it was also destroying about two thirds of the legitimate orders that reached it, and we did not know for months. Why the tests did not catch it This is the part I think generalises furthest. There were 143 unit tests over the validator and they all passed. There was a backtest across 31 real conversations and it passed too. Both of them stubbed the model call . That is a reasonable thing to do. Model calls are slow, expensive and non deterministic, and a test suite that hits a live API is a test suite nobody runs. So the tests supplied a fixed verdict and asserted that the validator routed it correctly. Which it did, perfectly, every time. ::: principle A test that stubs the model tests your routing. It cannot tell you anything about detection. If the component under test contains a model, the only measurement that means anything is a replay against the real one. ::: The backtest was worse, and more subtly so. It injected the model's claims and checked what the validator did with them — so it was measuring the same thing the unit tests measured, with more ceremony. It looked like an end to end validation and was not one. Finding a ground truth that needed no judgement The thing that unlocked this was realising there was an oracle

t: The instrument is usually the bug
s: A collection of cases where the measurement was wrong and the system was fine. If a number surprises you, the first hypothesis should be that the number is wrong.
p: When a metric is surprising, verify the metric before investigating the system. A number you cannot falsify is not a measurement.
b: A surprising share of the worst bugs I have worked on were not in the system. They were in the thing measuring the system, and the system was fine. This is worth naming as a category, because the instinct on seeing a strange number is to go and investigate the strangeness. That instinct spends a day on a problem that does not exist often enough to be worth a habit against. Eight of them The cost dashboard was wrong by 3.8×. Cached tokens were being priced as an addition to input tokens rather than a discounted subset. Reported spend was almost four times actual. Full entry /ahmedamer/lessons/cost dashboard overstated by 3.8x/ . du reported 296 KB for a directory that added 466 MB to an image. Sparse files have an allocated size and an apparent size, and a build context archives the apparent one. Full entry /ahmedamer/lessons/du lies about sparse files/ . Date bucketing silently returned nothing. The database's timezone tables were not loaded, so the framework's date truncation functions returned null, collapsing every date bucketed aggregate into a single empty bucket. Charts were not wrong, they were blank, and a blank chart reads as "no data" rather than "broken query." Three separate models in this system now exist specifically to bucket dates in application code and persist a real date column. The verification command failed on correct data. The tool that checks the latency instrumentation reported mismatches — and it was the tool that was broken, not the data. Partitioning by the condition that makes its comparison unambiguous settled it: single turn conversations, 232

t: Which direction does your guard fail?
s: The single most consistent principle I have arrived at: things on the customer's path fail open, things that verify correctness fail closed. Nearly every serious incident I have worked on is that rule applied backwards.
p: Never block a customer; always break a build. Decide a guard's failure direction before you write it, and put the reason in the code.
b: Every guard fails. That is not a criticism of guards — it is a property of software that runs long enough. The question that turns out to matter is not whether it fails but which way , and that is a decision somebody makes, or fails to make, at the moment the guard is written. I did not start with a rule. I arrived at one after enough incidents shared a shape. The rule Things on the customer's path fail open . Things that verify correctness fail closed , loudly, with a non zero exit. Never block a customer. Always break a build. Everything below is why, and where it gets uncomfortable. Failing open, on the path A customer is in a conversation, waiting. Every component between their message and the reply has the same obligation: if you break, get out of the way. So the prompt injection classifier, if it errors, lets the message through. The message ordering gate, if its store is unreachable, stops gating. The order validator, if it cannot run, allows placement and sends an alert. The cost accounting, if its schema is behind the code, swallows the failure rather than taking down the turn. Model resolution, if the database is unreachable, falls back to a default rather than refusing to pick. Each of those is a decision to accept a small, bounded risk — an injection gets through, an order goes unvalidated — rather than a certain, total failure, which is a customer who gets nothing. The uncomfortable part is that this is genuinely a security trade off, and I want to be honest about it rather than present it as free. s: Joined as an AI intern to work on generative AI use cases. Fourteen months later the work is production systems engineering, and most of what I learned came from things breaking in ways I had not imagined.
b: I joined as an AI intern in July 2025 and now work as an AI engineer on the same product. The title changed; more usefully, what I think the job is changed. The product is a multi tenant conversational commerce platform: customers order food over WhatsApp, an agent handles the conversation and takes payment, and the order appears in the restaurant's point of sale system. Several established food and beverage brands run on it. It is a team product with a team architecture, led by our AI manager. What follows is scoped to what I owned or found, and where something was a collective design I have tried to say so rather than absorb it.
